title: China's Soaring Chemical Exports Threaten a New Trade War Front
excerpt: A Rhodium Group report finds China near half of global output in key chemicals, with its share of India's PVC market up from 3 percent to 45 percent in five years and Europe's plant closures accelerating.
body:
• China has nearly doubled capacity in parts of its chemicals industry in five years and now accounts for about half of global output in some products, a Rhodium Group report for the US Chamber of Commerce found.
  • China's share of India's PVC market jumped from 3 percent in 2020 to 45 percent in 2025, squeezing out Japanese, South Korean and Taiwanese suppliers — and pressuring Indian producers.
  • European chemical capacity marked for closure rose six-fold, from 2.9 million tonnes in 2022 to 17.2 million tonnes in 2025.
  • The EU opened three anti-dumping investigations into Chinese chemicals in September, and Beijing answered with a probe of its own — chemicals are becoming the next front in the trade wars.

The trade war is moving beyond electric vehicles and semiconductors. A Rhodium Group report published on Monday, prepared for the US Chamber of Commerce and reported by the Financial Times, finds that China has nearly doubled its chemicals capacity in some segments in five years and now produces about half of global output of certain products — a build-out that is displacing rivals in Europe, India and emerging markets alike.

The scale of the build-out

Between 2020 and 2025, Chinese output of key plastics ingredients rose sharply: styrene up 97 percent, ethylene 80 percent, polyethylene 75 percent, polypropylene 71 percent and PVC 15 percent. Exports remain under 10 percent of China's total chemicals production, but shipments of four of those five products grew by more than 40 percent a year on average over the period. Jeremy Smith, the Rhodium analyst who authored the report, says Chinese producers are displacing foreign rivals across supply chains — rising in advanced economies, replacing imports at home, and outcompeting incumbents in faster-growing emerging markets.

India's PVC market shows the shift

For Indian industry, one figure captures the change. China's share of India's PVC market climbed from 3 percent in 2020 to 45 percent in 2025, while the combined share of Japan, South Korea and Taiwan fell from 56 percent to 34 percent. PVC is a construction and infrastructure staple, so the shift feeds directly into the cost base of Indian builders — and into the margins of Indian resin producers competing against Chinese supply priced by an industry where, the report notes, profits have fallen for four years and up to 31 percent of producers are lossmaking.

"Gas prices in Europe are six times as high as the United States. How can you compete?"

— Joerg Wuttke, partner, DGA Group

Europe's closures, and the retaliation cycle

Europe is absorbing the sharpest blow. Chemical capacity marked for closure there rose from 2.9 million tonnes in 2022 to 17.2 million tonnes in 2025 — a six-fold increase, with the total doubling in the past year alone — as high energy costs compound the pressure from low-cost Chinese supply. The chemicals fight is now feeding the wider dispute over China's trade surplus, which is on track this year to exceed the 2025 record of $1.2 trillion. The European Union opened three anti-dumping investigations into imports from China in September; Beijing responded with its own anti-dumping probe into a European chemical export used in dyes and pharmaceuticals.

China's commerce ministry did not immediately comment on the report. In July, it defended the country's rising exports, saying competitiveness partly reflects the energy crisis that has lifted production costs in Europe. Analysts note that low-cost Chinese chemicals also move prices in markets China does not supply directly, because the chemicals travel embedded in finished goods — electronics, autos and appliances among them.

What happens next

The report lands as governments weigh how far trade defence should extend beyond the headline sectors of EVs, steel and solar. For India, the question is pointed: its own chemicals and plastics producers face the same Chinese capacity wave that is closing plants in Europe, in a product — PVC — where Chinese suppliers now hold nearly half the Indian market. Further anti-dumping actions, by Brussels, Washington or New Delhi, are the near-term variable to watch.
